title: Two DNS servers, one port 53
role: You look after a small office's Ubuntu 20.04 server and want it to run Pi-hole as the DNS filter for the whole network.

source.label: pi-hole/pi-hole #4816: Installation breaks Ubuntu's systemd-resolved (GitHub issue)

brief: You install Pi-hole. Its DNS engine, FTL, refuses to start, and its log says port 53 is already in use. Nothing else was installed on this box, so who is on port 53?

steps.situation: FTL exits a second after it starts. The office still uses the router for DNS, so nobody is affected yet.
steps.evidence:
$ sudo ss -lntup 'sport = :53'
Netid State  Local Address:Port   Process
udp   UNCONN 127.0.0.53%lo:53      users:(("systemd-resolve",pid=612,fd=12))
tcp   LISTEN 127.0.0.53%lo:53      users:(("systemd-resolve",pid=612,fd=13))

choices.text: Find the owner of port 53: ss for the PID, then systemctl status of its unit
choices.why: Port → process → unit. It is `systemd-resolved`, Ubuntu's own resolver, with its stub listener on 127.0.0.53. Now you know what any change will touch.
resolved starts at boot, before Pi-hole. You get the same error a few minutes later.

choices.text: Move Pi-hole to port 5353 and carry on
choices.why: It starts, but clients only ask port 53. Your DNS filter answers nobody.

steps.situation: Both want port 53: resolved for the host itself, Pi-hole for the whole office. How do you share it?

choices.text: Turn off only the stub (DNSStubListener=no) and point /etc/resolv.conf at the non-stub file
choices.why: That is the full job, as the maintainer described it: resolved keeps working for the host, and port 53 is free for Pi-hole.

choices.text: Keep the stub on 127.0.0.53 and bind Pi-hole only to its own addresses
choices.why: Users in the thread did this, with `bind-interfaces` in a dnsmasq file. Both run, each on its own address. You must remember that the host asks resolved, not Pi-hole.
The port is free, but the host has no resolver until Pi-hole runs. One user could no longer pull the Pi-hole Docker image.
systemd restarts the service, and you have learned nothing about who owns it.

steps.situation: On a second server a colleague let the installer do it its own way. That host now resolves nothing: apt update fails, ping example.com fails.
steps.evidence:
$ systemctl status systemd-resolved | grep -i stub
... DNSStubListener= is disabled, but /etc/resolv.conf is a symlink to /run/systemd/resolve/stub-resolv.conf ...
$ ls -l /etc/resolv.conf
lrwxrwxrwx 1 root root 39 /etc/resolv.conf -> ../run/systemd/resolve/stub-resolv.conf
$ grep nameserver /etc/resolv.conf
nameserver 127.0.0.53

choices.text: Read resolved's warning and repoint the symlink to /run/systemd/resolve/resolv.conf
choices.why: The installer turned the stub off but left the host asking 127.0.0.53, where nothing listens now. resolved told you so in its status.

choices.text: Write a nameserver line into /etc/resolv.conf with echo
choices.why: You write through the symlink into a file resolved generates. It works until resolved rewrites it.
Pi-hole isn't the problem. The host's own resolver setup is half changed.

steps.situation: The host resolves again and Pi-hole runs. The router still hands out its own address as DNS.

choices.text: Test both paths before you switch DHCP: the host's lookups, and a query from a client to the server
choices.why: `resolvectl status` and `dig` on the host, then `dig @192.0.2.10 example.com` from a laptop. Switch DHCP when both answer.

choices.text: Switch DHCP now; people will tell you if it fails
choices.why: If it fails, the whole office loses DNS at once, and you find out from the help desk.

choices.text: Ubuntu is unsuitable: reinstall the server with another distribution
choices.why: A maintainer disagreed with dropping Ubuntu: many installs work. The fix is one setting and one symlink.

debrief.what_happened: In July 2022 a user reported that installing Pi-hole (v5.11.4, FTL v5.16.1) on Ubuntu 20.04 broke the host's own DNS. The installer sets `DNSStubListener=no` in `/etc/systemd/resolved.conf`, keeps a `.orig` copy and restarts resolved. But `/etc/resolv.conf` still links to the stub file, so the host keeps asking 127.0.0.53, where nothing listens, and resolved warns about exactly that. Maintainer dschaper showed that FTL fails with `Address already in use` while the stub holds port 53, and said the installer did "half the job": the symlink must also point at the non-stub file. The issue was labelled Bug: Confirmed in August 2022 and was still open when read. Users shared other ways: keep the stub and run Pi-hole on 127.0.0.1 and the LAN address, or add `bind-interfaces` in `/etc/dnsmasq.d/`. One user who turned resolved off could not pull the Pi-hole Docker image until they turned it back on.
lessons: `Address already in use`: find the owner (port → PID → unit) before you change anything.
On Ubuntu, 127.0.0.53 is systemd-resolved's stub; /etc/resolv.conf is usually a symlink to it.
If you turn the stub off, repoint /etc/resolv.conf in the same change.
Test DNS from the host and from a client before you hand the server to DHCP.
